claims.statement: EFRAG's cost-benefit analysis reports that its July 2023 survey across 13 Member States and more than 4,400 respondents found ESG requests reaching 8.5% of micro, 31.1% of small and 43.4% of medium enterprises, with estimated handling cost per request of EUR 2,100, EUR 4,700 and EUR 7,100 respectively. This evidences a measurable administrative loss, but not a purchase of the proposed service.

The same analysis says most observed requests were simple questionnaires, costs were relatively limited, and respondents made limited use of consultants or online platforms; similar information can also reduce the incremental cost of multiple requests. This directly weakens any assumption that every request supports a high service fee.

EFRAG's ex-ante model projected that by 2028 about 26% of EU SMEs would receive an ESG request and only 14% of that requested group would receive more than one; these are projections based on pre-Omnibus assumptions, not observed Polish repeat demand.

The 2025 VSME recommendation says a sustainability report is prepared annually if the large undertaking or bank requires an annual update, and it lets unchanged datapoints refer to the prior report. The annual renewal trigger is therefore counterparty-dependent rather than an automatic obligation on the SME.

Directive (EU) 2026/470 gives protected undertakings of up to 1,000 employees a right to decline CSRD-reporting requests above the voluntary-standard cap, but expressly does not oblige them to provide sustainability information and does not cover requests for other purposes such as due diligence or risk management.

On 3 July 2026 the Commission announced adoption of a voluntary standard based on VSME and said it was being submitted to Parliament and Council scrutiny, with application only after that scrutiny; the exact current operative status and market implementation are not established by the announcement.

EFRAG's late-2025 self-selected survey had 282 respondents, only 20% classed as users; 16% of users had fully used VSME information, 36% partially, 34% intended to use it and 14% did not use it. This is early adoption evidence, not proof of broad requester acceptance or Polish acceptance.

EFRAG respondents reported that many counterparties request information beyond VSME, especially supply-chain due diligence, Scope 3, product carbon footprints, business conduct and EU Taxonomy information. A VSME-only passport therefore does not eliminate bespoke mappings.

EFRAG supplies a free, open-source Excel template and XBRL converter with calculations, validation and machine-readable export; Poland's Ministry of Finance publicises the Polish-language template and locally verified translation. Basic form filling and format conversion are consequently commodity capabilities.

CDP provides a standardized disclosure platform used by large purchasing organizations and banks; it says roughly 45,000 suppliers were requested through its Supply Chain program in 2025 and that request recipients answer supply-chain questions in addition to the main questionnaire.

EcoVadis states that it has rated more than 175,000 companies, screened 3 million suppliers and enables one assessment to be shared across a customer network, with standardized comparative ratings and buyer-facing workflows.

Siemens reports that its own Corporate Responsibility Self-Assessment is an integral supplier-qualification questionnaire, with mandatory assessments for certain suppliers and reassessment every three years. This is direct buyer evidence of a recurring procurement gate using a buyer-specific process.

In EFRAG's 2025 market-acceptance survey, 23% of preparers took less than one week, 49% took one to three weeks and 29% took more than a month to prepare or gather VSME data; respondents highlighted reliable data collection and unclear calculation methods as practical problems. Evidence chasing is therefore a substantial delivery-risk variable.

EFRAG's consultation and field-test analysis expects many SMEs to use accountants, consultants or platforms, and identifies trained accountants as an adoption factor. That supports accountants as plausible delivery partners, but does not evidence referral appetite, exclusivity, conversion or customer-acquisition cost in Poland.

EFRAG estimated first-year total Basic Module cost near EUR 4,000 for smaller preparers and EUR 7,500-12,800 for larger preparers, with about half that cost in later years; it also estimated material internal work even when outsourced. These benchmarks show a serviceable burden but do not establish the proposed venture's labor hours or margin.

Statistics Poland counted 2.3745 million non-financial enterprises in 2024, including 2.3078 million microenterprises; small and medium enterprises were 2.0% and 0.6% of the total. Poland has a large absolute SME denominator, but the release does not identify suppliers receiving sustainability requests.

The Polish enterprise count and EU request-incidence evidence make a nontrivial top-down pool plausible, but applying EU-wide incidence mechanically to all Polish enterprises would overstate a reachable market without sector, export, large-buyer, bank-request and accounting-channel filters.
No evidence establishes what percentage of Polish buyers, tender administrators or lenders will accept a venture-produced VSME passport as a complete substitute for their own questionnaire.

No quoted, paid pilot, purchase order, signed letter of intent or Poland-specific willingness-to-pay study validates SME payment of 2,500-8,000 PLN initially, 1,500-4,000 PLN for refreshes, or 300-1,000 PLN per mapping.

No accounting office, lender adviser, procurement consultant or industry cluster is shown to have agreed to refer, resell or white-label the service, and no lead volume, conversion rate, sales cycle, commission or acquisition cost is known.

The venture has no measured founder or reviewer hours, document-chasing distribution, software and secure-storage cost, error-remediation cost, channel commission, support burden, contribution margin, cash conversion or capacity per five-hour founder day.

No executed customer service agreement, data-processing agreement, permission to reuse anonymized mappings, retention right, audit right, liability allocation or transfer right exists; access to each SME's evidence remains revocable and customer-controlled.

Although the standard supports counterparty-requested annual updates, there is no cohort evidence for refresh purchase rate, mapping frequency, logo retention, annual contract renewal or revenue retention for this offer.

The proposed 1,000-client and 4 million PLN revenue scenario is arithmetic rather than evidence: no reachable segmented denominator, acquisition throughput, contribution margin, retention, founder ownership dilution, valuation multiple or time-to-scale supports a path to 5 million PLN founder net worth.

The statutory cap improves VSME relevance for requests made specifically to satisfy CSRD reporting, but official guidance and market evidence show that other-purpose requests and additional datapoints remain possible; reusable acceptance is therefore bounded rather than universal.

Absent an endorsed requester network or exclusive customer contracts, the proposed evidence-source relationship is replaceable: the official template is free and open, while CDP and EcoVadis already control buyer-facing networks, standardized workflows and shareable records at scale.

The documented one-week-to-over-one-month preparation range and evidence-collection friction are compatible with a tightly bounded pilot but not yet with scalable part-time delivery; the founder's five-hour daily ceiling makes measured document completeness and exception rates decisive.
